source.note: No official answer sheet. The coursework's own numbers (motor parameters, specs, the student's controller gains) give derived cases; the measured rig data gives reality checks; the student's portfolio answers are claims.

parameters.rigModel: Coursework model + the info sheet's ±10 V drive limit + Coulomb friction T_c = 1.7 mNm fitted on the open-loop run only (then tested on the closed-loop runs).

concepts.title: The mechanical time constant JR/(K² + RD) sets the speed of response, not L/R
Overlay the model on measured data and measure the misfit (RMS)
A steady-state gap means a missing static term (friction), not a wrong inertia
PI velocity control: Kp sets speed, τi removes the steady-state error
The ±10 V limit: linear margins can't see saturation and integral wind-up
Position is the integral of speed: you must brake before you arrive
Nested loops: outer loop ~5× slower than the inner loop
Phase advance adds lead at the crossover frequency
Friction gives a proportional loop a dead zone; integral action removes it

misconceptions.text: The motor responds in L/R = 30 µs because that is the electrical time constant.
A heavier flywheel (bigger J) is why the rig settles at a lower speed.
A good phase margin guarantees a good step response on the real rig.
A PI loop leaves a steady-state error of a few rad/s (the portfolio's 2.5 and 2 rad/s).
A higher outer gain is always better; the bandwidth rule is optional.
The PA stops short because it has low gain at low frequency (a linear loop with an integrating plant has zero steady-state error at any gain).
Overshoot is measured from the axis you can see (the cropped plot), not from where the step started.

claims.claim: Output 1.2: the design model's 5 V step, overlaid on the rig data, matches it.
claims.why: The shape after the zero crossing matches (4.4 rad/s RMS with the student's 0.12 s shift), but RigData.mat is a −5 V → +5 V reversal starting at −157.5 rad/s, not a step from rest, and the model settles at 163.8 rad/s against the rig's 158.6. Coulomb friction of 1.7 mNm explains the gap (RMS 4.5 → 1.3 rad/s over the full reversal).
The info sheet gives 4.73×10⁻⁵. A transcription slip: it moves the time constant from 139.7 ms to 140.3 ms (0.4 %), far below what the rig data can resolve.
Kp(1 + 1/(τi·s)) with Kp = 0.13, τi = 0.1 s, exactly as in DCmodel_v1_with_PI_controller.slx and start_MSD_SIM.m. Phase margin 85°, crossover 31 rad/s, no phase crossover (infinite gain margin).
The linear model gives 2.9 %. With the info sheet's ±10 V limit (a ±75 rad/s reversal asks for 19.5 V) it would be 5.3 %.
The rig run is a −75 → +75 rad/s reversal (a 150 rad/s step). The plot's y-limits hide the bottom half, so the overshoot was taken against 75 instead of 150: 8.9 % of 75, but 4.4 % of the real step.
Integral action drives the error to zero: the model's is 0.00 rad/s and the rig's mean error over its last 100 ms is under 0.1 rad/s. The ±1.5 rad/s you can see is encoder noise, not an offset.

claims.claim: The system's performance looks really good … acceptable overshoot
claims.why: It works, but the phase margin is 85° against a 60° target, a slower and safer design than asked for. The ±75 reversal saturates the 10 V drive (the Simulink model has no limit), and that saturation is why the rig overshoots more than the model.

claims.claim: PA controller (0.688·0.005·9 s + 0.688) / (0.005 s + 1), designed for ~60° phase margin
claims.why: It gives 55.4° of phase margin, close to the target. But the lead peaks (53°) at 1/(τ√k) = 66.7 rad/s while the loop crosses over at 12.7 rad/s, so only 26° of lead is used where it matters. K_PA would need to be about 5× higher to put the crossover on the lead's peak.

claims.claim: PA model: rise 0.11 s, overshoot 16 %, settling 2.17 s
claims.why: Rise 0.107 s and overshoot 16.4 % are right. 2.17 s is the clock time on the plot (the step is at 1.63 s); the settling time from the step is 0.56 s.

claims.claim: The rig data has an undershoot due to the nature of the PA controller which has a low gain at low frequency
claims.why: It is a steady-state error (the rig parks at 0.79 rad), not an undershoot. A linear loop around an integrating plant has zero steady-state error at any gain, so low gain alone can't do it. Friction can: 0.688 V/rad × 0.21 rad = 0.14 V is too little to unstick the motor. The friction measured in task 1.2 predicts a dead zone of ±0.22 rad, and the rig's 0.21 rad miss is inside it.

It works on the rig (model vs rig 0.046 rad RMS, phase margin 58.6°), but it breaks the info sheet's rule of thumb: the outer loop's bandwidth (29.7 rad/s) is only 1.1× slower than the inner loop's (33.7 rad/s), not 5×. G ≈ 5.5 meets the rule.
1.322 s is the clock time on the plot (the step is at 1.0 s). From the step, the model settles (±2 %) in 0.22 s and the rig in 0.33 s.
The model's 9 % is right (9.3 %). The rig's 11 % has the same cropped-plot error as task 2: the run is a −1 → +1 rad reversal, and the peak is 10.7 % of 1 rad but 5.3 % of the real 2 rad step.

claims.claim: The nested loop is more robust than the PA … seen in the stability of the two systems
claims.why: Their stability margins are almost equal (58.6° vs 55.4°). The rig shows the real difference: the nested loop's integrator pushes through friction to exactly 1.000 rad, while the PA parks 0.21 rad short.

cases.note: Steady state: ω = K·V / (K² + R·D). Time constant: J·R / (K² + R·D). The electrical L/R is 4600× faster.
The info sheet's J (4.73e-5) instead of the script's 4.75e-5.
The gain that meets the info sheet's 5× bandwidth rule.
